title: Fit a hand cone into a contracted practice hand's fist without forcing its fingers open
instruction: Fit the hand cone into this practice hand: across the palm, wide end at the little-finger side, with all four fingers curled round it and the thumb outside. Don't force the fingers open. Then let go and move clear.
context: Many older people in care homes live with a hand clenched into a fist after a stroke, or with dementia, Parkinson's disease or long immobility. Left closed, the fingers stiffen for good, the palm sweats and the skin breaks down, nails dig in, and washing the hand hurts. A hand cone held in the fist keeps the palm open, clean and dry and slows the contracture, so it is fitted every day as part of routine positioning care. That work falls to nursing assistants (O*NET 31-1131.00, 1.5 million US workers), who turn, reposition and exercise residents with restricted mobility, and to home care aides. Prying contracted fingers open hurts the resident and can tear skin; the accepted way lets the wrist relax into flexion so the fingers loosen by themselves (tenodesis), places the cone, and lets the wrist return so the fingers close round it.
setup: Positions in m from the arm bases' midpoint, x forward, y left. Pillow: 17 x 34 x 6 cm firm polyurethane foam (about 35 kg/m3) in a cotton cover, centred at (0.37, 0.10), orange tape L-marks at its corners. On it a life-size practice left forearm, palm up along +y, wrist axis at (0.37, 0.07): a 50 mm PVC tube with a foam sleeve, sand-ballasted to 1.1 kg, held by two hook-and-loop straps. Hand: PLA prints (STL files in the task folder) on 3 mm steel pins; palm 9.5 cm long, 8.5 cm across the knuckles, 7.0 cm at the wrist, 2.4 cm thick; thumb fixed, adducted along the index side. Fingers proximal/middle-distal, the latter one piece bent 35 deg at the DIP: index 42/24+20, middle 45/27+22, ring 43/26+21, little 38/21+19 mm. Pin stops: MCP 20-110 deg, PIP 40-120 deg flexion. Flexor per finger: braided line from the fingertip through 1.5 mm palm-side channels (8 mm from the MCP pin, 6 mm from the PIP pin), over a 24 mm radius pulley on the palm side of the wrist, then 60 mm of 4 mm silicone cord (300 N/m) with a braided check loop beside it that goes taut after 15.5 mm stretch (then 2.5 N/mm), to the forearm through a 10 N peak-hold force gauge (e.g. Sauter FK 10), one per finger; about 1 N each at rest. Extensor per finger: elastic cord (300 N/m, 0.6 N at rest) in a covered groove on the back of the hand and forearm, 8 mm from the MCP, 3 mm from the PIP, over a 20 mm radius wrist pulley, so the back of the hand lies flat on the pillow. Wrist: pin hinge, flexion 0-85 deg, stopped at straight, torsion return spring 0.04 N m/rad. Hand cone: rigid printed PLA, 13 cm long, 5.0 to 3.0 cm across, 40 g, on its side between two 8 x 12 mm wooden rails on a 10 x 8 x 12 cm plywood box at (0.315, -0.15), wide end towards the robot overhanging the box by 2.5 cm.
scoring: Ruler, phone photos from the side and above, the four gauges' peak marks; held 2 s, both grippers 3 cm clear of hand and cone, forearm within 2 cm of its tape marks. 1.0 when the cone lies across the palm (resting on it, axis within 25 deg of the knuckle line, wide end at the little-finger side) with every fingertip resting on its upper half. 0.5 when the cone rests in the palm with at least two fingertips on its upper half. 0.25 when the cone rests in the palm. 0 if any finger's gauge peaked over 5 N, the forearm left its marks by 2 cm at any time, the cone fell below the pillow's top, or any other end state, including a gripper within 3 cm.
reset_notes: Lift the cone out by its wide end with the wrist flexed (never pry), let the wrist return so the fist clenches, and reset each gauge's peak mark to zero. Check the pillow sits in its tape marks and the straps are snug. Every 10 trials, check each flexor cord: with the wrist straight and the fist clenched, the gauge reads 0.8-1.2 N (the sim settles at 0.9 N); hold the wrist at 45 deg with a protractor and check every fingertip lifts at least 4 cm off the palm. Re-tension a cord that reads outside, or replace its silicone section. Replace the cone's box rails if the cone can roll.
fidelity: Rigid printed parts on pins; every physics step each cord's tension is computed from its path length (wrist and finger angles) and applied as joint torques: a geometric spring law, no timed or rule events. Each gauge is its flexor's peak tension, the measure of harm: forcing the clenched fingers open stretches the check loop and passes 5 N. No silicone skin (rigid contact, friction 0.8, a 12 mm torsional patch on the palm); the thumb is fixed.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (valid run); scripted demo: 1.0 (432 steps)
